questions.q: What is a structure in C++?
o: A function that returns multiple values simultaneously
A block of memory allocated only at run time
A collection of functions that share the same name
A collection of simple variables of different data types grouped under one name
questions.e: A structure groups simple variables, possibly of different data types, under a single name. The individual variables it holds are called its members.

questions.q: The individual variables that make up a structure are referred to as its:
o: members
tags
operators
instances
questions.e: The data held inside a structure are called the members of the structure.

questions.q: Which keyword introduces a structure definition in C++?
o: structure
struct
class
record
questions.e: The keyword 'struct' introduces a structure definition; the structure name (tag) follows the keyword.

questions.q: In a structure definition, the name that immediately follows the struct keyword is called the:
o: access specifier
destructor
member
structure name (tag)
questions.e: The identifier following the struct keyword is the structure name, also called the tag.

questions.q: How must every structure definition be terminated in C++?
o: With the keyword end
With a semicolon after the closing brace
With a colon after the closing brace
With a matching parenthesis
questions.e: The member declarations are enclosed in braces, and each structure definition must end with a semicolon.

questions.q: Which operator is used to access the members of a structure variable?
o: The dot operator, e.g. part.cost
The address-of operator
The arrow operator only
The scope resolution operator
questions.e: Members of a structure are accessed using the dot operator, for example part.cost accesses the cost member of the part variable.

questions.q: Can two different structures contain members having the same name?
o: Only if one structure is nested inside the other
No, member names must be globally unique
Yes, two different structures may contain members of the same name
Only if the members are of different data types
questions.e: Two different structures may contain members of the same name because member names are scoped to their own structure.

questions.q: Which statement about initializing data members inside a structure definition is correct?
o: Only floating-point members can be initialized in the definition
No member of any kind may ever be initialized anywhere
Data members cannot be initialized in the structure except const static integral data members
All data members can be freely initialized in the definition
questions.e: Data members cannot be given initial values inside a structure definition; the only exception is const static integral data members.

questions.q: Given 'struct part { int modelnumber; float cost; };', what are the data types of modelnumber and cost respectively?
o: float and float
int and int
float and int
int and float
questions.e: In the part structure, modelnumber is declared int and cost is declared float, demonstrating that a structure can hold members of different types.

questions.q: A structure named Room contains two members, length and width, each of type Dist (itself a structure with feet and inches). To reach the feet of the length, which access is correct?
o: dining::length::feet
dining.feet.length
dining.length.feet
dining.length->feet
questions.e: With nested structures, the dot operator is chained: dining.length.feet selects the length member of the Room, then the feet member of that Dist.

questions.q: When a structure variable is initialized as 'dist d2 = {30, 40};', what do 30 and 40 represent?
o: The values assigned in order to the structure's members feet and inches
Two arguments passed to a constructor
The array size and starting index
The memory address and offset of the structure
questions.e: Brace initialization assigns values to members positionally, so 30 goes to the first member (feet) and 40 to the second member (inches).

questions.q: Can objects (variables) of a structure be passed to and returned from functions?
o: Neither passing nor returning is permitted
Yes, structure objects can both be passed to functions and returned from them
They can be returned but never passed in
They can be passed to functions but never returned
questions.e: Just as ordinary variables are passed to functions, structure objects can be passed to functions, and they can also be returned from functions.

questions.q: A structure is described as a collection of simple variables. What key characteristic distinguishes those variables?
o: They must all be pointers
They must all be constants
They may be of different data types
They must all be of the same data type
questions.e: The defining feature of a structure is that it collects simple variables that may be of different data types under one name.

questions.q: To convert an amount given as an integer number of pence into pounds (for example 365 pence into 3.65 pounds), what arithmetic relationship is used?
o: Divide the pence by 100 to get a floating-point number of pounds
Subtract 100 from the pence
Add 100 to the pence
Multiply the pence by 100
questions.e: 365 pence equals 3.65 pounds, so the integer pence value is divided by 100 to produce the equivalent floating-point number of pounds.

questions.q: In the area-calculation menu, which formula corresponds to the area of a triangle?
o: Pi * R squared
L squared
L * W
questions.e: The area of a triangle is base times height times one half (B*H*0.5); L*W is a rectangle, L squared is a square, and Pi*R squared is a circle.

questions.q: What is function overloading?
o: Declaring one function that calls itself repeatedly
Giving a single function an unusually large number of statements
Declaring several functions with the same name but different signatures
Declaring functions with different names but identical bodies
questions.e: Function overloading is the practice of declaring functions of the same name but with different signatures (different number or types of parameters).

questions.q: When an overloaded function is called, how does the compiler select which version to run?
o: By comparing the argument list of the call with each function's parameters
By choosing the function with the fewest statements
By choosing the function that was declared first
By comparing the return types of the functions
questions.e: The correct overloaded function is selected by comparing the argument list of the call against each candidate's parameters; return type is not used.

questions.q: Is overloading functions that differ only by return type allowed in C++?
o: Yes, but only inside a class
Yes, return type alone is enough to overload
No, overloading functions with different return type is not allowed
Yes, but only for functions returning int or float
questions.e: Overloading based solely on a different return type is illegal in C++; the functions must differ in their parameter lists.

questions.q: Among these declarations, which one is illegal because it only differs from an existing function by return type: 'void func(float a, float b);' already exists.
o: void func(int a, char b);
int func(float a, float b);
void func(float a, int b);
void func(int a);
questions.e: 'int func(float a, float b);' has the same parameter list as the existing 'void func(float a, float b);' and differs only by return type, which is not a valid overload.

questions.q: Function overloading is typically employed in which situation?
o: Only for functions that return pointers
Only when a function takes no parameters
Wherever a different type of data needs to be handled by similarly-named operations
Only when a function must call itself
questions.e: Overloading is used where different types of data must be dealt with, such as one version handling integer data and another handling float for precision.

questions.q: What is a default argument?
o: A parameter that can never be given a value
A parameter value supplied automatically when the caller omits that argument
An argument that must always be provided by the caller
The return value produced when a function fails
questions.e: A default argument gives a parameter a preset value that is used automatically if the caller does not supply that argument.

questions.q: Which rule governs which arguments may be given default values?
o: Only the first argument may be defaulted
Any single argument in the middle may be defaulted
Only trailing arguments may be defaulted
All arguments must be defaulted or none may be
questions.e: Only trailing arguments may be defaulted; you cannot have a default argument followed by a non-default argument.

questions.q: Once you begin using default arguments within a function's parameter list, what must be true of the remaining arguments?
o: The remaining arguments must be removed
The next argument must be non-default
Exactly one more argument may be non-default
All subsequent arguments in that list must also be defaulted
questions.e: As soon as a default argument is used, every subsequent argument in that function's parameter list must also be given a default value.

questions.q: Given 'void repchar(char ch='x', int val=5);', what happens when it is called as repchar( ) with no arguments?
o: ch takes 5 and val takes 'x'
ch takes 'x' and val takes 5
The call fails to compile
Both parameters remain uninitialized
questions.e: With no arguments supplied, both defaults apply: ch becomes 'x' and val becomes 5.

questions.q: For 'void repchar(char ch='x', int val=5);', what values are used for the call repchar('w')?
o: The call is illegal because only one argument is given
ch takes 'x' and val takes 'w'
Both ch and val take 'w'
ch takes 'w' and val takes the default 5
questions.e: The single supplied argument fills the first parameter (ch='w'), and the omitted trailing argument uses its default, so val=5.

questions.q: In C++, a class is best described as:
o: A function that returns a structure
A reserved keyword with no members
A synonym for an array of integers
An expanded concept of a structure and a mechanism for creating user-defined data types
questions.e: A class is an expanded concept of a structure and a mechanism for creating user-defined data types, containing both data members and member functions that operate on them.

questions.q: Which keyword is generally used to declare a class in C++?
o: object
class
struct
define
questions.e: Classes are generally declared using the keyword class, followed by the class name and the member declarations in braces.

questions.q: Beyond holding data, what additional capability does a class provide compared with a plain collection of data?
o: It can contain member functions that operate on its data members
It can only store integers
It prevents any access to its data
It automatically prints its members
questions.e: Unlike a bare data grouping, a class can contain member functions (operations) that act on its data members.

questions.q: In C++, the term 'object' refers to:
o: A function with no return value
A synonym for a data type
A reserved keyword
An instance of a class
questions.e: An object is an instance of a class; for example, from a class smallobj you might create objects s1 and s2.

questions.q: By default, what is the access level of the members of a C++ class?
o: protected
private
friend
public
questions.e: By default all members of a class are private, whereas by default all members of a struct are public.

questions.q: By default, what is the access level of the members of a struct in C++?
o: static
public
protected
private
questions.e: In a struct the default access is public, which is the main distinction from a class where the default is private.

questions.q: What is stated to be the main difference between a struct and a class in C++?
o: The default access specifier of their members
Whether they can contain member functions
Whether they can have constructors
The maximum number of members they may hold
questions.e: In C++ struct and class are almost interchangeable; both can have member functions, constructors, destructors and base classes. The only difference is the default access: public for struct, private for class.

questions.q: Which access specifier makes a member usable anywhere, without the restrictions imposed by private or protected?
o: static
public
private
protected
questions.e: A public member can be used anywhere without the access restrictions that private or protected impose.

questions.q: A member declared private can be accessed by which of the following?
o: Members of derived classes but not the class itself
Only static functions anywhere
Any function in the program
Only the members and friends of the class
questions.e: A private member can be used only by the members and friends of that class.

questions.q: How does a protected member differ from a private member with respect to derived classes?
o: A protected member is also accessible to members and friends of derived classes, unlike a private member
A protected member is accessible from anywhere, unlike a private member
A protected member cannot be accessed by the class's own members
There is no difference between protected and private
questions.e: A private member is limited to the class's own members and friends, whereas a protected member additionally allows access to the members and friends of derived classes.

questions.q: Which listed difference between a C-language structure and a C++ class is correct?
o: Both C structures and classes provide built-in data hiding
A C structure defaults to private members
A C structure binds data and functions, while a class holds only data
A C structure contains only data, while a class binds both data and member functions
questions.e: A C-language structure contains only data, whereas a C++ class binds together both data and member functions; the C structure also provides no data hiding and defaults to public members.

questions.q: A friend of a class X is best described as:
o: A function or class that is not a member of X but is granted the same access to X as X's members
A member function that can only read public data
A global variable shared by all objects of X
A class that inherits publicly from X
questions.e: A friend of a class X is a function or class that is not a member of X but is granted the same access to X as the members of X have.

questions.q: Given a class with a private member and public functions setdata and showdata, how would you call setdata on an object s1 to store 100?
o: setdata(s1, 100);
s1->setdata->100;
smallobj::setdata(100);
s1.setdata(100);
questions.e: Public member functions are invoked on an object with the dot operator, so s1.setdata(100) stores 100 through the object s1.

questions.q: Which of the following is a genuine feature classes provide that C-language structures do not?
o: The ability to store floating-point numbers
The ability to hold multiple members
Data hiding
The use of the dot operator
questions.e: Data hiding is provided by classes but not by C-language structures; both can hold multiple members of various types and use the dot operator.

questions.q: Within a class declaration, what follows an access specifier such as public: or private:?
o: The name of the object to be created
The class's base classes only
The return type of the constructor
The members and functions governed by that access level
questions.e: An access specifier introduces a section of the class; the members and member functions declared after it are governed by that access level until another specifier appears.

questions.q: A constructor is a member function that has:
o: Any name chosen by the programmer
The same name as its class
The same name as its class prefixed by a tilde
The reserved name 'main'
questions.e: A constructor is a member function whose name is exactly the same as the class name, for example Part() for a class Part.

questions.q: What does a constructor return?
o: Nothing; it has no return value, not even void
An integer status code
A pointer to the newly created object
void, which must be written explicitly
questions.e: A constructor does not return any value; you specify neither void nor any other return type for it.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a constructor?
o: Comparison of two objects
Printing the object's data
Initialization of the object's variables
De-allocation of memory
questions.e: Constructors are used to initialize the variables of an object and are called at the point an object is created.

questions.q: When is a constructor called?
o: Once when the program terminates
At the point an object of the class is created
Only when the object is destroyed
Only when a member function is explicitly invoked
questions.e: A constructor is called automatically at the moment an object of its class is created.

questions.q: A default constructor is characterized by the fact that it:
o: Has a name different from the class
Returns an integer
Takes exactly one argument
Takes no arguments
questions.e: A default constructor is one that takes no arguments.

questions.q: How is a destructor's name written relative to the class name?
o: The class name in all capital letters
The class name prefixed by a tilde (~)
The class name prefixed by 'delete'
The class name followed by parentheses only
questions.e: A destructor is a member function with the same name as its class, prefixed by a tilde (~), for example ~Part().

questions.q: What is the usual purpose of a destructor?
o: To de-allocate memory and perform cleanup when an object is destroyed
To overload arithmetic operators
To return a value describing the object's state
To initialize member variables when an object is created
questions.e: Destructors are typically used to de-allocate memory and do other cleanup for a class object and its members when the object is destroyed.

questions.q: Which statement about a destructor's arguments and return type is correct?
o: It takes no arguments but returns an integer
It takes no arguments and has no return type
It may take several arguments but returns nothing
It takes one argument and returns void
questions.e: A destructor takes no arguments and has no return type.

questions.q: In the class 'Counter { Counter(){count=0;} Counter(int n){count=n;} };', what value does count hold immediately after creating an object as 'Counter c2(5);'?
o: It is uninitialized
questions.e: Creating c2(5) invokes the second constructor Counter(int n), which sets count=n, so count becomes 5.

questions.q: Two constructors in the same class, one taking no arguments and one taking an int, are an example of:
o: Operator overloading
A default argument
A friend function
Constructor overloading (same name, different signatures)
questions.e: Providing multiple constructors with the same class name but different parameter lists is overloading applied to constructors, distinguished by their argument lists.

questions.q: Can a constructor be given arguments used to initialize members with specific values?
o: Only the destructor may take arguments
Yes; a parameterized constructor such as Counter(int n) initializes members from its arguments
Only if the constructor returns a value
No; constructors can never take arguments
questions.e: Besides the default (no-argument) constructor, a class may have parameterized constructors such as Counter(int n) that initialize members from the supplied arguments.

questions.q: A friend function is best defined as:
o: A member function shared by two classes
A member function that can access only public members
A function automatically generated for every class
A function that is not a member of a class but has access to the class's private and protected members
questions.e: A friend function is not a member of the class, yet it is granted access to the class's private and protected members; it is a normal external function given special access privileges.

questions.q: Are friend functions considered members of the class they befriend?
o: Yes; they are ordinary member functions
Only when the class has no other members
No; they are normal external functions given special access privileges
Yes; but only if declared in the private section
questions.e: Friend functions are not considered class members; they are normal external functions that are merely given special access to the class.

questions.q: How should a friend function be called?
o: Using the scope resolution operator with the class name
As an ordinary function, not using the dot operator
Always using the dot operator on an object
Using the arrow operator on a pointer
questions.e: Because friend functions are not members of any class, they should not be called using the dot operator; they are called like ordinary functions.

questions.q: Can a single function be declared as a friend of more than one class?
o: Yes, and it must be declared as a friend in each such class
Only if the classes are related by inheritance
No, a function may befriend only one class
Yes, but it need only be declared in one of the classes
questions.e: A function can be a friend of more than one class, but it must be declared as a friend inside each class where that access is wanted.

questions.q: In which section of a class may a friend declaration be placed?
o: Only the protected section
Either the private or the public section; it makes no difference
Only the private section
Only the public section
questions.e: A friend declaration can be placed in either the private or the public section of a class with no difference in effect; the stated standard practice is to place it in public.

questions.q: What special ability do friend functions provide that ordinary non-member functions lack?
o: The ability to return multiple values
The ability to be called without any arguments
Access to the private data of one or more classes to which they are friend
Automatic memory de-allocation
questions.e: Friend functions can access the private data of one or more classes to which they are declared friend, which no other non-member function can do.

questions.q: A friend function 'check(bacteria, virus)' needs access to the private members of both the bacteria and virus classes. What must be done?
o: It must be made a member of one of the two classes
It need only be declared friend in the bacteria class
It must be declared as a friend inside both the bacteria class and the virus class
It must be declared friend in a third, unrelated class
questions.e: For a function to access the private data of two classes, it must be declared as a friend in each of those classes; declaring it in only one is not sufficient.

questions.q: Consider 'void check(bacteria b, virus v)' where bacteria sets life=1 in its constructor and virus sets life=0 in its constructor. Given the test prints 'A bacteria is alive.' when b.life==1 and 'A virus is alive.' when v.life==1, which messages appear?
o: No messages at all
'A virus is alive.' only
'Something is alive' and 'A bacteria is alive.'
'Something is alive' and 'A virus is alive.'
questions.e: The bacteria constructor sets life=1 and the virus constructor sets life=0. So b.life==1 makes the 'Something is alive' and 'A bacteria is alive.' lines print, while the virus line (requiring v.life==1) does not.

questions.q: In a program where a class car declares 'friend car display(car);' and display sets x.speed=60 and increments x.model, what does display prove a friend function can do?
o: Create new car objects without a constructor
Only read, never modify, the private members
Read and modify the private members speed and model of a car object
Access public members but not private ones
questions.e: Because display is a friend of car, it can both read and modify the private members speed and model (setting speed to 60 and incrementing model), which a non-friend external function could not do.

questions.q: A friend function declared inside class Tutorial as 'friend int Add(int x);' creates a local Tutorial object whose private data member equals 5 and returns data + x. What does Add(4) return?
questions.e: The local Tutorial object initializes its private data to 5 through the constructor, and Add returns data + x = 5 + 4 = 9, which is possible only because Add is a friend and can read the private data.

questions.q: In a program with 'class virus;' written before the bacteria class, what is the purpose of that line?
o: It creates a virus object
It makes virus a friend of bacteria automatically
A forward declaration so the name virus is known before it is fully defined
It deletes the virus class
questions.e: 'class virus;' is a forward declaration that introduces the name virus so it can be referenced (for example in a friend declaration) before the full definition of the virus class appears.

questions.q: A friend function that receives a class object by value, modifies the object's members, and returns it (such as 'car display(car x)') affects the caller's original object how?
o: The function cannot modify the object at all
The caller must assign the returned object back to see the changes, e.g. mine = display(mine)
The caller's original object is modified directly with no assignment needed
The changes are lost and can never be retrieved
questions.e: Because the object is passed by value, the function works on a copy; the modified copy is returned, so the caller writes mine = display(mine) to capture the changes into the original object.

questions.q: What does operator overloading allow in C++?
o: Creating brand-new operator symbols such as +*
Overloading operators only for basic data types
Changing the number of operands a built-in operator takes
Redefining the meaning of most existing operators for user-defined objects
questions.e: Operator overloading lets you redefine the meaning of almost all existing operators so they behave in a chosen way for instances of a class.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT permitted with operator overloading?
o: Implementing an operator as a member function
Redefining the + operator for a user-defined class
Giving an operator more than one meaning
Introducing a completely new operator such as +*
questions.e: You cannot introduce new operators; only existing operators can be overloaded. For instance, an operator such as +* cannot be created.

questions.q: How does the compiler distinguish between the different overloaded meanings of an operator?
o: By the total number of operators in the program
By the order in which the overloads were written
By examining the types of the operator's operands
By examining the operator's return type
questions.e: The compiler tells the different meanings apart by examining the types of the operator's operands.

questions.q: Which keyword declares a function that specifies what an operator symbol means for a class?
o: virtual
friend
operator
overload
questions.e: The operator keyword declares a function stating what an operator symbol means when applied to instances of a class; overloaded operators are implemented as functions.

questions.q: Overloaded operators are implemented as:
o: Macros
Functions
Structures
Global variables
questions.e: Overloaded operators are implemented as functions, using the form return_type operator operator_symbol(parameter-list).

questions.q: Operator overloading works with which of the following?
o: Both user-defined objects and basic data types equally
Only pointer types
User-defined objects only, not basic data types
Basic data types only, not user-defined objects
questions.e: Operator overloading works only with user-defined objects; it does not apply to basic (built-in) data types.

questions.q: Operator functions can be implemented as:
o: Either global functions or member functions (global ones are often friend functions)
Only member functions
Only static functions
Only global functions
questions.e: Operator functions can be global or member functions; when implemented as global functions they are often friend functions.

questions.q: Consider a class Counter that starts count at 0 (default) or n (parameterized) and overloads ++ to do count++. If c2 is created as Counter c2(5) and then ++ is applied to it twice, what is c2's count?
questions.e: c2 begins at 5 through the parameterized constructor, and each ++ increments count by one; applying ++ twice gives 5+2 = 7.

questions.q: A class Distance holds feet and inches and overloads + so that when the summed inches reach 12.0 or more, 12 is subtracted from inches and feet is incremented. Adding a distance of 3 feet 9.0 inches to 4 feet 5.0 inches gives:
o: 7 feet 14.0 inches
8 feet 2.0 inches
8 feet 14.0 inches
7 feet 2.0 inches
questions.e: The inches add to 9.0+5.0 = 14.0, which is at least 12.0, so 12 is subtracted (2.0 inches) and feet is incremented: 3+4+1 = 8, giving 8 feet 2.0 inches.

questions.q: When the += operator is overloaded for a Distance class as a member function taking one Distance argument (as in dist1 += dist2), what does the operation do?
o: Creates and returns a brand new Distance without changing dist1
Swaps the values of dist1 and dist2
Adds dist2's feet and inches into dist1, normalizing when inches reach 12.0
Subtracts dist2 from dist1
questions.e: The overloaded += adds dist2's feet and inches directly into dist1 (feet += d2.feet, inches += d2.inches) and carries over when inches reach 12.0, modifying dist1 in place.

questions.q: Why should overloaded operators be used only when their meaning is obvious?
o: Because the compiler forbids more than one overload
Because overloading always slows the program down
Because overloaded operators cannot be documented
Because misused overloading can make a program more difficult and harder to understand
questions.e: While overloading can make a program more readable, it can also make it harder to understand if the meaning is not obvious; the guidance is to use similar meanings and otherwise use a named function.

questions.q: The general form used to declare an overloaded operator function is:
o: return_type operator_symbol(parameter-list) operator
operator_symbol return_type(parameter-list)
overload operator_symbol return_type(parameter-list)
return_type operator operator_symbol(parameter-list)
questions.e: An operator function is written as return_type operator operator_symbol(parameter-list), for example Distance operator + (Distance d2).

questions.q: When the overloaded + is written as a member function 'Distance operator + (Distance d2)' and called as dist3 = dist1 + dist2, which object supplies the left operand?
o: The object on which the operator is called (dist1), accessed through its own members
A temporary object created by the compiler
Neither operand; both come from d2
The argument d2 (dist2)
questions.e: For a member operator function, the left-hand operand is the object the function is called on (dist1), whose members are used directly, while the right-hand operand is passed as the argument d2.

questions.q: Memory allocation refers to:
o: The speed at which a program executes
The number of functions a program declares
The fixed amount of memory a program requires to store its variables and data structures
The process of compiling source code
questions.e: Memory allocation is the amount of memory required by a program to store the values of its variables and data structures.

questions.q: C++ provides which two types of memory allocation to hold program variables?
o: Temporary allocation and permanent allocation
Static memory allocation and dynamic memory allocation
Local allocation and friend allocation
Stack allocation and register allocation
questions.e: C++ offers two kinds of memory allocation for holding variable contents: static memory allocation and dynamic memory allocation.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes static memory allocation in C++?
o: It is allocated by the system only at run time
Its size can be changed freely at run time
It has fixed size and fixed location that do not change during the program's lifetime
It requires pointers and the new operator
questions.e: In static memory allocation the compiler allocates memory that has a fixed size and fixed location, neither of which changes during the lifetime of the program.

questions.q: A statically declared array such as 'int myarray[10];' has what limitation?
o: It can grow automatically as more elements are added
Its size is fixed and cannot be changed while the program is running
It is deleted automatically after each function call
It can only hold floating-point values
questions.e: A static array's size is fixed at compile time; once declared with a particular size it cannot be changed while the program is running, which motivates dynamic arrays.

questions.q: When is dynamic memory needed rather than static memory?
o: When the memory size is known before compilation
When no pointers are available
When the program uses only constants
When a variable amount of memory can only be determined during execution time
questions.e: Dynamic memory is required when a variable amount of memory is needed that can only be determined during execution (run) time.

questions.q: Dynamic memory in C++ is allocated using which operator?
o: static
new
malloc
delete
questions.e: In C++ the new operator is used to dynamically allocate memory at run time, for example new int or new int[40].

questions.q: What does the new operator return, which must be captured?
o: The number of bytes allocated
The value stored at the allocated space
The address of the allocated space
A boolean success flag
questions.e: The new operator returns the address of the allocated space, so that address must be captured in a pointer.

questions.q: To create a dynamic array of 40 integers and store its address, which statement is correct?
o: int ptr = new int[40];
int * ptr = new int[40];
int * ptr = int[40];
int[40] ptr = new int;
questions.e: An integer pointer captures the address returned by new: int * ptr = new int[40]; creates an array of 40 integers and stores its starting address in ptr.

questions.q: Which operator is used to de-allocate dynamically allocated memory in C++?
o: remove
new
free
delete
questions.e: The delete operator de-allocates dynamic memory in C++; for an array the syntax is delete [] pointer_name;.

questions.q: What is the correct syntax to de-allocate a dynamically allocated array through a pointer named array?
o: delete [] array;
remove [] array;
free array;
delete array[];
questions.e: For a dynamic array the de-allocation syntax is delete [] pointer_name; e.g. delete [] array;.

questions.q: What happens if dynamically allocated memory is never released?
o: It speeds up the program
It converts into static memory
It becomes a memory leak
It is automatically reclaimed by the compiler
questions.e: Dynamic memory is created on the free store; if it is not released it becomes a memory leak, so it must be de-allocated for reuse.

questions.q: Why is static memory not a concern for manual de-allocation?
o: Static memory is never actually used
Static memory always causes leaks
Static memory is released with the delete operator
Static variables and arrays are automatically handled by the compiler, which has determined their scope and lifetime
questions.e: You never need to worry about releasing statically allocated memory because static variables and arrays are handled automatically by the compiler, which already knows their scope and lifetime.

questions.q: Creating dynamic memory is described as involving which two steps?
o: Delete an existing pointer, then declare a new class
Declare a constructor, then declare a destructor
Create a statically allocated pointer, then create dynamic space and store its address in the pointer
Overload the new operator, then overload delete
questions.e: The two steps are: first create a statically allocated pointer (e.g. int * ptr;), then create dynamic space and store its address in that pointer.

questions.q: In which region of memory are static arrays reserved, according to the material?
o: Register memory
Read-only program memory
The free store (heap)
Stack memory
questions.e: Static arrays are declared prior to execution and are reserved in stack memory, whereas dynamic memory is created and released with new and delete on the free store.

questions.q: In a DynamicArray class whose constructor runs 'array = new int[arraysize];' and fills array[i] = i, what values does an object created with size 5 hold after construction?
questions.e: The constructor loops from i=0 up to arraysize and assigns array[i] = i, so a size-5 array is filled with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

questions.q: In the DynamicArray class, what does the ChangeSize member function do first before allocating a new array?
o: It copies the old array into a backup
It deletes the previously allocated dynamic array with delete [] array;
It calls the destructor directly
It prints the current array
questions.e: ChangeSize first releases the previously allocated array using delete [] array; and only then allocates a new array of the requested size and reinitializes it.

questions.q: In the DynamicArray class, what cleanup does the destructor ~DynamicArray() perform?
o: It deletes the dynamic array with delete [] array;
It sets the array pointer to a new array
It increases the array size
It prints a farewell message
questions.e: The destructor's job is to free the dynamically allocated array, which it does with delete [] array; when the object is destroyed.

questions.q: The C++ standard string class provides which kind of operations?
o: String manipulation such as copying, searching, and replacing
Only file input and output
Only memory de-allocation
Only integer arithmetic
questions.e: The standard string class provides a number of string manipulation operations such as copying, searching, and replacing, and supports overloaded operators like +, +=, and ==.

questions.q: Which set of operators is overloaded for use with the C++ string class?
questions.e: The string class allows the use of overloaded operators such as +, +=, and == for concatenation, append-assignment, and comparison.

questions.q: What does the definition 'string str(8, 'x');' create?
o: A string containing eight 'x' characters
A string containing the two characters 8 and x
An empty string reserved for 8 characters
A string of length 8 filled with spaces
questions.e: The constructor string str(8, 'x'); builds a string consisting of eight 'x' characters.

questions.q: When reading into a string with the extraction operator (cin >> str), input is terminated by:
o: A semicolon
The end of the file only
A white-space character (the input is delimited by white space)
A comma only
questions.e: The overloaded >> reads a string from the keyboard delimited by white-space characters; when a delimiter is encountered the input operation is terminated.

questions.q: Which function reads an entire line of text, including spaces, into a string object?
o: str.at(0);
getline(cin, str);
str.length();
cin >> str;
questions.e: getline is overloaded for strings; getline(cin, str); reads a whole line of text and saves it into a string object, unlike >> which stops at white space.

questions.q: Which member function returns the number of characters in a string str?
o: str.at()
str.find()
str.length() or str.size()
str.empty()
questions.e: Both str.length() and str.size() return the size (length) of the string str.

questions.q: What does str.empty() return?
o: The first character of the string
The index of the last character
The number of characters in the string
true (1) if the string is empty and false (0) otherwise
questions.e: str.empty() informs whether the string is empty, returning true (1) if it is empty or false (0) if it is not.

questions.q: Which expression appends the text 'bomb' to the end of a string str?
o: str.append("bomb"); or equivalently str += "bomb";
str.assign("bomb");
str.compare("bomb");
str.erase("bomb");
questions.e: str.append("bomb"); appends 'bomb' to str, and the equivalent shorthand using the overloaded operator is str += "bomb";.

questions.q: Which member function assigns the value of str2 to str1 (equivalent to str1 = str2;)?
o: str1.compare(str2);
str1.assign(str2);
str1.swap(str2);
str1.append(str2);
questions.e: str1.assign(str2); assigns the value of str2 to str1, which is the alternative to writing str1 = str2;.

questions.q: What does str.at(4) return?
o: The length of the string up to index 4
True if index 4 exists
The character at index 4 of the string str
A substring of the first four characters
questions.e: str.at(4) returns the character located at index 4 of the string str.

questions.q: When str1.compare(str2) is used and the two strings are equal, what value is returned?
o: The length of str1
questions.e: str1.compare(str2) returns an integer: 0 if the strings are equal, a positive number if str1 is greater, and a negative number if str2 is greater than str1.

questions.q: For str1.compare(str2), what does a positive return value indicate?
o: The two strings are equal
Both strings are empty
str1 is greater than str2
str2 is greater than str1
questions.e: A positive result from str1.compare(str2) means str1 is greater; a negative result means str2 is greater, and 0 means they are equal.

questions.q: Which function retrieves a substring of str2 (for example str1 = str2.substr(StartIndex, LengthOfIndex);)?
o: substr
rfind
erase
swap
questions.e: str2.substr(StartIndex, LengthOfIndex) retrieves a substring of str2, which can be assigned into another string.

questions.q: What does str1.swap(str2) do?
o: Concatenates str1 and str2
Compares str1 and str2
Copies str2 into str1 without changing str2
Swaps the values of str1 and str2
questions.e: str1.swap(str2) exchanges the values of the two strings str1 and str2.

questions.q: What does str.find("is") return?
o: The number of times 'is' occurs in str
True if 'is' is present
The last index of 'is', searching backward
The starting index of the string 'is' within str, searching forward
questions.e: str.find("is") performs a forward search and returns the location (starting index) of 'is' within str.

questions.q: How does str.rfind("is") differ from str.find("is")?
o: rfind returns the character instead of the index
rfind counts occurrences instead of locating one
rfind performs a backward search rather than a forward search
rfind ignores case while find does not
questions.e: str.find performs a forward search for the starting index of the target, whereas str.rfind performs a backward search for it.

questions.q: What does str.find_first_of("abcd") locate?
o: The first occurrence in str of any character in 'abcd'
The last character of str
The number of vowels in str
The first occurrence of the whole word 'abcd'
questions.e: str.find_first_of("abcd") locates the first occurrence in str of any single character contained in 'abcd'; find_last_of locates the last such occurrence.

questions.q: The replace function is called as str.replace(index, 3, "The"). What do its three arguments represent?
o: The location to begin replacing, the number of characters to replace, and the replacement string
The string, the search text, and the count
Three separate replacement strings
The start index, the end index, and the replacement string
questions.e: str.replace takes three arguments: the location in the string at which replacement begins, the number of characters to replace, and the replacement string.

questions.q: What does str.erase(6) do?
o: Erases everything from position 6 to the end of the string, including position 6
Erases six characters starting from position 0
Erases only the single character at position 6
Erases the first 6 characters of the string
questions.e: str.erase(6) erases everything from and including the character at position 6 through to the end of str.

questions.q: What does str.erase(5, 8) do?
o: Erases from position 5 to position 8 only
Erases the whole string starting at position 8
Erases from and including position 5 for the next 8 characters (indices 5 through 12)
Erases exactly two characters at positions 5 and 8
questions.e: str.erase(5, 8) erases from and including the character at position 5 and continues for 8 characters, covering indices 5 through 12. (The source notes describe this as 'the next 7 characters (Index 5-12)', which is internally inconsistent, since 8 characters span indices 5 to 12.)

questions.q: Why are static local variables used?
o: When a variable should be destroyed after every statement
When a variable must be shared between two different programs
When a variable must never be initialized
When a function needs to remember the value of a variable between calls
questions.e: Static local variables are used when it is necessary for a function to remember a value of a variable across its calls.

questions.q: A static local variable has the visibility of an automatic local variable, but its lifetime is:
o: The same as a global variable (except it comes into existence only at the first call to its function)
The same as a register variable
Limited to a single statement
Only until the function first returns
questions.e: A static local variable has the visibility of an automatic local variable but a lifetime like a global variable, except that it does not come into existence until the first call to the function containing it.

questions.q: Which keyword begins the declaration of a static variable?
o: global
extern
const
static
questions.e: The declaration of a static variable begins with the keyword static.

questions.q: In the function 'float getavg(float newdata){ static float total=0; static int count=0; count++; total+=newdata; return total/count; }', why are total and count declared static?
o: So they cannot be modified
So they become visible outside the function
So they are destroyed and recreated on each call
So they retain their accumulated values between successive calls, allowing a running average
questions.e: Declaring total and count static lets them persist across calls, so each call adds to the running total and count and returns the cumulative average.

questions.q: For a static data member of a class, how many copies exist relative to the objects of that class?
o: A single copy is shared by all objects of the class
One copy per member function
No copy exists until the program ends
One separate copy per object
questions.e: A static member variable is used when only one copy of a variable should be shared by all objects of the class, rather than each object having its own copy.

questions.q: Which access levels may a static class member be declared with?
o: public only
private only
public, private, or protected
It cannot have an access level
questions.e: Static members can be declared public, private, or protected.

questions.q: What is the visibility and lifetime of a static class member?
o: Visible nowhere and never created
Visible everywhere with a lifetime of a single function
Visible only within one function and destroyed on return
Visible only within the class but with a lifetime of the entire program
questions.e: A static class member is visible only within its class, but its lifetime is the entire program.

questions.q: A static data member requires two separate statements. Where does the variable's definition appear?
o: Inside every constructor
Outside the class, in the same way as a global variable (e.g. int foo::count = 0;)
Inside the class body only
Inside the main function only
questions.e: A static data member needs a declaration inside the class definition and a separate definition outside the class, written like a global variable, for example int foo::count = 0;.

questions.q: In a class foo whose constructor executes count++ on a private static member count (defined as int foo::count = 0;), what will getcount() report after three objects f1, f2, f3 have been created?
questions.e: Because count is static and shared, each of the three constructor calls increments the single shared count, so after creating f1, f2, and f3 the value is 3.

questions.q: Which restriction applies to a static member function?
o: It can access only non-static members
It can access only static members plus data and functions outside the class
It can access all members including non-static ones
It cannot access any members at all
questions.e: A static member function can access only static members and data and functions outside the class, whereas a non-static member function can access all of those plus static data members.

questions.q: What advantage does a static member function offer regarding class instantiation?
o: It can only be called after many objects exist
It can be called even when the class has not been instantiated as an object
It cannot be called at all
It can be called only from the destructor
questions.e: Static member functions become useful whenever functions are needed that are accessible even when the class is not instantiated; a static function can be called without creating an object.

questions.q: A non-static member function can be called only:
o: After the class has been instantiated as an object
When the program terminates
Before any object is created
From within a static function
questions.e: A non-static member function can be called only after instantiating the class as an object, in contrast to a static member function which can be called even without an instance.

questions.q: In a class gamma with a static member total and an instance member id, where the constructor does total++ then id=total, what are the id values of three objects g1, g2, g3 created in that order?
o: All three have id equal to 3
1, 2, and 3 respectively
3, 3, and 3 respectively
0, 1, and 2 respectively
questions.e: The shared static total increments to 1, 2, then 3 as each object is constructed, and each object copies the current total into its own id, so g1.id=1, g2.id=2, and g3.id=3.

questions.q: How is a static member function called using the class name in the gamma example (gamma::showTotal())?
o: Only through a pointer using the arrow operator
With the class name and the scope resolution operator, without needing an object
It cannot be called by name at all
Only through an existing object using the dot operator
questions.e: A static member function such as showTotal can be invoked with the class name and scope resolution operator, gamma::showTotal(), because it does not require an instance of the class.

questions.q: Inheritance in object-oriented programming allows a programmer to:
o: Delete the members of an existing class
Combine two unrelated programs into one file
Designate that a new class inherits the members of an existing class instead of writing them anew
Prevent any class from reusing another class's members
questions.e: With inheritance, when creating a class the programmer can specify that the new class should inherit the members of an existing class, rather than writing entirely new data members and functions.

questions.q: In an inheritance relationship, the existing class whose members are inherited is called the:
o: Abstract class
Friend class
Derived class
Base class
questions.e: The existing class that is inherited from is called the base class, while the new class that inherits from it is called the derived class.

questions.q: The new class that inherits the members of an existing class is called the:
o: Static class
Base class
Parent class
Derived class
questions.e: The new class formed through inheritance is the derived class; the class it inherits from is the base class.

questions.q: Given the pairing Base class 'Shape' with derived classes, which set are described as its derived classes?
o: GraduateStudent and CollegeStudent
Circle, Triangle, Rectangle, Cube, Square
Faculty and Staff
CheckingAccount, CurrentAccount, SavingAccount
questions.e: The Shape base class is paired with the derived classes Circle, Triangle, Rectangle, Cube, and Square; Faculty/Staff derive from Employee and the account types derive from Account.

questions.q: For the base class Account, which classes are given as its derived classes?
o: GraduateStudent, CollegeStudent
Faculty, Staff
CheckingAccount, CurrentAccount, SavingAccount
Circle, Triangle, Rectangle
questions.e: Account is the base class for CheckingAccount, CurrentAccount, and SavingAccount.

questions.q: The class Employee is shown as the base class for which derived classes?
o: Circle and Square
CheckingAccount and SavingAccount
Faculty and Staff
GraduateStudent and UnderGraduateStudent
questions.e: Employee is the base class from which Faculty and Staff are derived.

questions.q: Can a single class act as both a base class and a derived class?
o: Yes; inheritance relationships form treelike hierarchies where a class can be base, derived, or both
No; a class is permanently either base or derived
Only static classes can be both
Only if it has no members
questions.e: Inheritance relationships form treelike hierarchical structures, and within them a class can be a base class, a derived class, or both.

questions.q: Which syntax correctly derives a class CountDn publicly from a base class Counter?
o: class CountDn inherits Counter { ... };
class CountDn :: Counter { ... };
class CountDn : public Counter { ... };
class CountDn extends Counter { ... };
questions.e: Public inheritance is written class CountDn : public Counter { ... };, placing the access keyword and base class name after a colon.

questions.q: In a base class Counter, the member 'count' is declared under 'protected:' so that a derived class CountDn can decrement it with --count. Why must count be protected rather than private?
o: Protected members are accessible to derived classes, whereas private members are not
Private members cannot be integers
Protected members are faster to access than private ones
Protected members are automatically static
questions.e: A derived class can directly access protected members of its base class but not private ones, so declaring count as protected lets CountDn modify it.

questions.q: When a derived class defines its own showData() but still needs the base class version, how can it call the base class function explicitly (base class Bahria)?
o: Bahria::showData();
showData::Bahria();
base.showData();
this.Bahria.showData();
questions.e: The base class version is invoked with the scope resolution operator and the base class name, e.g. Bahria::showData();, even from inside the derived class's own showData.

questions.q: What does multiple inheritance allow?
o: A single base class to have many derived classes
A class to be derived from more than one base class
A class to inherit from itself
A function to belong to two classes
questions.e: Multiple inheritance means a class can be derived from more than one class, for example class C : public A, public B { };.

questions.q: Which declaration correctly shows class C inheriting publicly from both class A and class B (multiple inheritance)?
o: class C : public A : public B { };
class C : public A, public B { };
class C : public A and B { };
class C inherits A and B { };
questions.e: Multiple inheritance lists each base class separated by commas: class C : public A, public B { };.

questions.q: What is the literal meaning given for 'virtual' in the context of virtual functions?
o: Existence in appearance but not in reality
Something that runs faster than normal
A function that cannot be called
A permanently constant value
questions.e: Virtual is described as meaning existence in appearance but not in reality; a virtual function is used to override the base class function.

questions.q: A C++ virtual function has which of these main features?
o: It is a friend function of two classes
It is a global function resolved at compile time
It is a static function that needs no object
It is a member function declared with the virtual keyword and resolved at run time
questions.e: A virtual function is a member function of a class, declared with the virtual keyword, usually with different functionality in the derived class, and its call is resolved at run time.

questions.q: Consider a base class Base with a non-virtual show() printing 'Base', and derived classes Derv1 and Derv2 each with their own show(). A Base* ptr is set to a Derv1 object then a Derv2 object, calling ptr->show() each time. What is printed?
o: Base and Base
Base and Derv2
Derv1 and Derv2
Derv1 and Base
questions.e: Without the virtual keyword, the call is bound at compile time to the pointer's type (Base), so ptr->show() prints 'Base' both times regardless of the object pointed to.

questions.q: Now suppose the same base class declares show() as virtual, and Base* ptr points first to a Derv1 object then to a Derv2 object, calling ptr->show() each time. What is printed?
o: Base and Base
Base and Derv1
Derv1 and Derv2
Derv2 and Derv1
questions.e: With show() declared virtual, the call is resolved at run time based on the actual object, so ptr->show() prints 'Derv1' then 'Derv2'.

questions.q: Choosing which function to call at run time, based on the actual object a pointer points to, is called:
o: Operator overloading
Late binding (dynamic binding)
Early binding (static binding)
Function overloading
questions.e: Deferring the decision until the program is running is called late binding or dynamic binding; choosing functions during compilation is called early binding or static binding.

questions.q: Choosing which function to call during compilation, in the normal way, is called:
o: Early binding (static binding)
Late binding (dynamic binding)
Run-time binding
Virtual binding
questions.e: Selecting functions during compilation is early binding, also called static binding; the run-time alternative enabled by virtual functions is late or dynamic binding.

questions.q: Why does adding the virtual keyword to a base class function cause the call decision to be deferred to run time?
o: Because the pointer type changes automatically
Because virtual functions must be static
Because the compiler cannot know which derived class the base pointer will actually point to
Because virtual functions are never compiled
questions.e: With virtual, the compiler does not know whether the pointer holds the address of a Derv1 or Derv2 object, so it arranges for the decision to be deferred until run time when the actual class is known.

questions.q: Regarding pointer compatibility, what is true of pointers to derived class objects?
o: Pointers to objects of a derived class are type compatible with pointers to objects of the base class
A base class pointer can never hold a derived object's address
Derived pointers can only point to base objects
Pointers cannot be used with class objects
questions.e: Pointers to objects of a derived class are type compatible with pointers to objects of the base class, which is why a Base* can be assigned the address of a derived object.

questions.q: What is an abstract class?
o: A class that cannot have derived classes
A class that can only be instantiated once
A class that is never meant to be instantiated and exists only to be a parent of derived classes
A class with no members at all
questions.e: An abstract class is one you never want to instantiate objects of; it exists only to act as a parent of derived classes that will be used to create objects.

questions.q: An abstract class must consist of at least one:
o: Pure virtual function
Static member function
Friend function
Constructor with arguments
questions.e: An abstract class consists of at least one pure virtual function.

questions.q: How is a pure virtual function declared?
o: By adding =0 to its declaration, e.g. virtual void getData() = 0;
By declaring it as a friend
By adding the keyword static before virtual
By writing the function body as empty braces
questions.e: A pure virtual function has the expression =0 added to its declaration, for example virtual void getData() = 0;.

questions.q: What happens if you attempt to create an object of a class that contains a pure virtual function?
o: The class is converted to a struct
The function runs automatically
The compiler complains because you are trying to instantiate an object of an abstract class
An object is created but immediately destroyed
questions.e: Once a pure virtual function is placed in a class, attempting to create an object of that class causes the compiler to complain that you are trying to instantiate an object of an abstract class.

questions.q: If a derived class does not override the pure virtual function it inherits, what is the consequence?
o: It becomes a base class of the original
It automatically supplies a default body
It compiles but the function is skipped
It becomes an abstract class itself and cannot be instantiated
questions.e: Once a base class has a pure virtual function, every derived class from which you want to create objects must override it; a class that fails to override it becomes an abstract class itself and cannot be instantiated.

questions.q: In an abstract person class with pure virtual isOutstanding(), a student overrides it to return true when gpa > 3.5, and a professor overrides it to return true when numPubs > 100. For a student with GPA 1.2 and a professor with 712 publications, which one(s) are 'outstanding'?
o: Both of them
Only the professor
Only the student
Neither of them
questions.e: The student's GPA of 1.2 is not greater than 3.5 (not outstanding), while the professor's 712 publications exceed 100, so only the professor is outstanding.

questions.q: In the person hierarchy, objects are created dynamically with 'persPtr[n] = new student;' or 'new professor;' and later processed through the base pointer array. What makes each object's correct getData() and isOutstanding() run?
o: The functions are static and shared
The functions are virtual, so the correct derived version is chosen at run time through the base pointer
The base class versions always run regardless of object type
Each object is cast back to its type manually before every call
questions.e: Because getData() and isOutstanding() are virtual (pure virtual in the abstract base), calls made through the base class pointers are resolved at run time to the appropriate student or professor version.

questions.q: Virtual functions enable 'completely different functions to be executed by the same function call.' In the shapes example with an array of base pointers calling ptr[j]->draw(), what determines which draw runs?
o: The actual object each pointer points to (a ball's draw for a ball, a triangle's draw for a triangle)
The size of the pointer array
The order in which the pointers were declared
The name of the base class only
questions.e: With virtual functions, the same call ptr[j]->draw() runs the drawing function matching the actual object pointed to, so a ball object draws a ball and a triangle object draws a triangle.

questions.q: An exception is best described as:
o: A comment ignored by the compiler
A type of loop that never terminates
An unusual condition that affects the normal flow of a program
A normal instruction that always executes
questions.e: An exception is an unusual condition which affects the normal flow of a program.

questions.q: In exception handling, the code that intercepts an exception is called the:
o: monitor
trigger
handler
signal
questions.e: The code that intercepts an exception is called a handler.

questions.q: Exception handling is best described as:
o: A technique for allocating dynamic memory
A method of speeding up normal program flow
A way for a program to encounter an unusual situation and try to solve it
A way to overload operators safely
questions.e: Exception handling is a way in which a program encounters an unusual situation and tries to solve that situation.

questions.q: The unwanted errors that trigger exceptions and can be detected by a function may be of which kinds?
o: Only errors in comments
User, logic, or system errors
Only syntax errors caught by the compiler
Only formatting errors in output
questions.e: These unwanted errors could be user, logic, or system errors that can be detected by a function.
